stemMd:
The new ferry timetable was intended to **(i)** ______ the congestion at the harbour, but because it moved every departure into the same half-hour, it in fact **(ii)** ______ it.

**Blank (i):** alleviate / celebrate / investigate

**Blank (ii):** exacerbated / relieved / predicted
instructionsMd: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. Both blanks must be correct; there is no credit for a partially correct answer.
explanationMd:
The sentence is built on a plan that backfired: the timetable "was intended to" do one thing, "but ... in fact" did another.

**Blank (i) — the intention.** What would a harbour authority *intend* a new timetable to do about congestion? Reduce it. **"Alleviate"** means to make less severe.

**Blank (ii) — the result.** The "because" clause explains what went wrong: every departure was crowded into the same half-hour. Bunching all the traffic together makes congestion worse, and "but ... in fact" confirms the result reversed the intention. **"Exacerbated"** means made worse.

**The answer is alleviate and exacerbated.**

**How to check.** Read the finished sentence and confirm the two blanks are opposites, because "intended to ... but in fact" promises a reversal: *intended to ease it, in fact worsened it.* Then confirm the "because" clause supports the second word: crowding departures together is a cause of worse congestion, not better.

distractorRationale.blank1-c: "Celebrate" makes no sense as the purpose of a timetable. Nobody designs a schedule to praise congestion, and the reversal signalled by "but in fact" needs an intention that the bunched departures could defeat.
distractorRationale.blank1-b: "Investigate" is something a study does, not a timetable. A schedule of departures does not examine congestion, and the sentence's reversal ("but in fact") has nothing to reverse if the timetable was never meant to change the congestion.
distractorRationale.blank2-b: "Relieved" means the same as the intended outcome. "But ... in fact" announces that the result differed from the intention, and the "because" clause, all departures in one half-hour, describes a cause of crowding, not of relief.
distractorRationale.blank2-c: "Predicted" treats the timetable as a forecast. A timetable that moves departures changes the congestion rather than foretelling it, and the "because" clause explains a change in the congestion, not a forecast of it.

accessibilityText: A sentence with two blanks. The new ferry timetable was intended to blank one the congestion at the harbour, but because it moved every departure into the same half-hour, it in fact blank two it. For blank one choose among alleviate, celebrate and investigate. For blank two choose among exacerbated, relieved and predicted. Both blanks must be correct.

provenance.notes: Original two-blank Text Completion written for wave 7 as the easy anchor of the batch. The ferry and harbour are invented. Option ids carry blank1- and blank2- prefixes matching the answer key's columnIds. Not adapted from any ETS item.

review.notes: Author solved as alleviate and exacerbated, twice. Uniqueness: 'intended to ... but in fact' requires the two blanks to be opposed and the first to be a plausible aim; celebrate and investigate are not aims a timetable can have, relieved repeats the intention and so cancels the reversal, and predicted does not describe a change caused by moving departures. Checked all nine combinations. Awaiting blind independent solve; the author must not publish own work. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
